prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 rows toward higher y, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. The default recipe gives only 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples each, which is probably too few for exact builds. Fewer PPO epochs buy more samples, and smaller rollouts give more updates. So two candidates keep the starting network and test recipe changes (2 epochs vs 1). The third tests a structural idea that fits this task. A brick's outcome depends on which layer it lands on (the maximum build height under its footprint) and on whether the footprint cells at that layer are all target cells. So I score each placement separately per layer, using features shared across layers, and use a learned softmax gate over layers to pick the landing layer. That network uses fewer FLOPs than the starting one, so the budget does not shrink. It uses candidate A's recipe, so the two can be compared directly.

### Round 2
Every trial so far scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success: the starting net with 2 epochs, the starting net with 1 epoch, and a per-layer gated net. Recipe changes alone (1 to 2 epochs, 230k to 400k samples) did not help, so sample count is probably not the bottleneck. My working guess is that the policy cannot reliably tell which placements are exactly right, i.e. that the brick lands in missing target cells and seals nothing below. That needs clean per-column features pooled over each footprint. The starting net only gets them after two 3x3 convolutions that blur neighbouring cells. A second risk is collapse onto DONE: random placements score negative, DONE scores 0. Entropy is the lever that can be pulled legitimately against that. This round tests three things. (1) A column MLP feeding footprint pooling directly. (2) A learned 3x3 placement head with no pooling, which still works if the anchor convention differs from the one described. (3) Net (1) with higher entropy.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0, on both dev and training success. That includes two recipes (1 or 2 epochs), higher entropy, a per-layer network, a column MLP and a pooled head, and r2c2's anchor-agnostic 3x3 head. Seed noise cannot explain this. I see two likely causes. (1) Every network so far assumes action index t*Y*X + y*X + x lines up spatially with obs cell (y, x). If this world transposes or flips that mapping, no translation-equivariant head can learn, which would match the total failure. (2) Optimisation or credit assignment is too weak for exact builds at this budget. This round tests both. A adds a fully connected action head that can learn any cell-to-action mapping, on top of a local head. B adds one local head for each of the 8 flips and transposes of the grid. C keeps the standard alignment and changes only the recipe: longer horizon, lower lr, more updates.

### Round 4
All 9 trials (18 seeds) scored 0 on dev, and their train success was also 0. That covers the starting net with 1, 2 or 4 epochs, entropy 0.005 to 0.03, gamma 0.95 or 0.99, per-layer gates, learned 3x3 per-type heads (which work for any anchor), and 8 dihedral views. In the world as described, a simple local rule should be easy to learn and would complete many targets: place a 1x1 brick where the landing cell is missing, then DONE. So local nets that handle isometries and anchor offsets failing every time suggests this world differs in a way local structure cannot fit. The likely cause is a mapping from action index to cell that is not an isometry, possibly with scrambled observation cells too. The only global head so far (r3c1, FC behind a 256-unit ReLU bottleneck, plus a competing local head) is weak evidence against this. The last round therefore tests direct learned linear maps from cells to actions, with and without spatial convolutions.

## Trial it ended with
name: cell MLP + learned cell-to-action map
hypothesis: No spatial convolutions. A deep per-cell MLP computes whether each cell is a good landing spot. A full learned linear map (K*Y*X to n_place) assigns those scores to action indices, so the net works under any permutation of observation cells or action indices. It uses less compute than the starting net, lr 2e-3, 2 epochs. Refuted if train and dev success stay at 0. That would point to the reward or dynamics rather than the action mapping.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 3 guesses that the spatial alignment between observation and actions is off: "If this world transposes or flips that mapping" between action index and "obs cell (y, x)". Round 4 adds "possibly with scrambled observation cells too". So the text points at a spatial misalignment in what the agent observes. It never says that only the target channels are shifted, or that they are rolled 4 rows toward higher y with wraparound.
